analysis.one_liner: Lets Congress nullify federal agency rules with a simple resolution the president cannot veto.
analysis.headline: Four Republican senators introduced the bill in October 2015; it never received a hearing, a vote, or any action before Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have changed federal rulemaking so that when both chambers of Congress pass a "concurrent resolution" declaring what a law means, agencies could not issue rules that contradict it, and would have to rewrite any existing rule that does. Concurrent resolutions require only simple majorities in the House and Senate and are not sent to the president for approval or veto, so this would have let a congressional majority strike down regulations without the president's consent. The bill was referred to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee and received no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Industries regulated by federal agencies — banks, energy producers, manufacturers, pharmaceutical companies — would gain a fast, repeatable way to get rules they dislike invalidated. Instead of persuading the president to veto a repeal or winning a veto-proof two-thirds vote, a simple majority in both chambers could rewrite the meaning of a law after the fact. Anyone harmed by a specific regulation could lobby for a concurrent resolution instead of a new law.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a section to the Administrative Procedure Act barring agencies from issuing any rule that conflicts with a concurrent resolution Congress passes to "clarify" the meaning of a law, including whether a law delegated authority to the agency in the first place.
If an agency already has a rule in effect that conflicts with such a resolution, the agency must write new rules that conform to the resolution's interpretation.

Concurrent resolutions take effect without the president's signature, so under this bill a bare congressional majority could reinterpret a statute and force agencies to comply without any presidential check.
Supporters' rationale is that Congress, not unelected regulators, should decide what laws mean, and that concurrent resolutions offer a lighter-weight check on agency overreach than full legislation.

analysis.who_pays: People protected by federal rules — workers, consumers, investors, and communities affected by pollution or unsafe products — would bear the risk that their protections could be reversed by a simple majority vote in Congress, without the deliberation of a full legislative process and without a presidential veto as a backstop. Agencies would also face the operational cost of continually rewriting rules.

drawbacks.text: Because concurrent resolutions do not require the president's signature, the mechanism removes the normal check that a president must approve changes to how laws are carried out, letting a one-time simple majority rewrite the meaning of long-standing statutes.

The bill defines a "clarification" so broadly — including whether a law even delegated authority to an agency — that it could be used to invalidate rules after the fact rather than genuinely resolving ambiguity.
Agencies and courts would face uncertainty about the meaning of laws whenever Congress passed such a resolution, and agencies would bear the cost of rewriting rules each time a majority acted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Even taken on its own terms, the bill's benefit — giving Congress a tool to check agency interpretations — is outweighed by its design: it bypasses the president entirely, applies retroactively to rules already in effect, and defines "clarification" broadly enough that any regulation could be targeted. It also never advanced, so it produced no benefit. Had it become law, the practical effect would have been to make federal protections easier for a temporary congressional majority to reverse.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never took it up, so it never got a hearing or a floor vote before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Michael Enzi introduced the bill on October 22, 2015, with three Republican cosponsors: Senators Ayotte, Crapo, and Daines.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs.
No further action was ever taken; the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing system was left intact: federal agencies kept the authority to issue rules without congressional concurrent resolutions, and regulated industries did not gain the new fast-track tool to invalidate regulations they opposed. Ordinary people's existing regulatory protections remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing rules and the agencies that issue them

for.name: Sen. Michael B. Enzi
for.role: U.S. Senator from Wyoming; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Regulatory Authority Clarification Act of 2015 in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Kelly Ayotte, Mike Crapo, and Steve Daines
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only cosponsors it attracted.

against.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over administrative law and federal rulemaking
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never took it up — no hearing, no mark-up, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the 114th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four sponsors and the bill's three cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never advanced far enough for a recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have given these industries a new tool: lobby a simple congressional majority for a concurrent resolution and a rule they dislike gets struck down, without needing the president or a new law. Their gain would come directly at the cost of rules that protect workers, consumers, and the public.

Agencies would lose final authority over the meaning of the laws they enforce, forced to rewrite rules whenever Congress passed a resolution. This would serve the interest of industries seeking deregulation while reducing agencies' ability to carry out protective mandates.

industries.industry: Workers, consumers, and communities protected by federal rules
industries.note: This is the public interest the bill's defeat preserved: existing workplace, consumer, environmental, and financial rules could not have been reversed by a bare congressional majority. Its stake in the outcome is the mirror of the regulated industries' stake.
